1233.title: Truth
1233.hook: Pilate asks what truth is and walks out; the Dominicans made the word their motto
1233.howItsDone: Veritas appears on the shields and in the mottos of Dominican houses, schools and colleges; Dominicans connect it to study, preaching and the belief that Christ is the truth.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the order approved, and the first thing Dominic did was scatter his few friars. Your line was to the cities.

A Roman governor, early in the morning, in his own headquarters. A prisoner stands before him, hands tied, and says he came into the world to give testimony to the truth. The governor, Pilate, answers with a question people still ask at kitchen tables and in philosophy classes. In the Douay-Rheims: "What is truth?" Then John's Gospel adds a detail that's easy to miss. Pilate doesn't wait. He goes straight back out to the crowd. A question that large, and he walks out on it. Today, an order that decided to stay in the room. Its motto is one word: truth.
screen: `A GOVERNOR, A PRISONER, EARLY MORNING.` → `WHAT IS TRUTH?` → `HE DOESN'T WAIT FOR THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The word is veritas, Latin for truth, and the Dominicans carry it as their motto, on their crests and over their schools. In the Latin Bible a medieval friar read, Pilate's question is quid est veritas, what is truth. Someone later noticed a word game: rearrange the letters and you get est vir qui adest, it is the man who is here. The answer was standing in front of Pilate the whole time. That's the Christian claim under the motto. In John's Gospel, Jesus says, "I am the way, and the truth, and the life." So for a Dominican, truth isn't only a set of correct statements. It's someone to follow. And it isn't meant to stay private. Jesus promises in John that "the truth shall make you free." Free, not cornered. That shapes how the truth gets told. Paul's letter to the Ephesians has a phrase for it: "doing the truth in charity." Either one alone goes wrong. Truth without charity becomes a weapon; charity without truth becomes flattery. The order's own history shows how hard it is to keep the two together, and in a few days this path will look at that honestly. But the motto still points at a simple daily task: say what is real, as someone who wants the other person to be free.
screen: `VERITAS: THE DOMINICAN MOTTO.` · `QUID EST VERITAS? EST VIR QUI ADEST.` · `TRUTH IS SOMEONE TO FOLLOW.` · `DOING THE TRUTH IN CHARITY.` · then, large: `THE TRUTH SHALL MAKE YOU FREE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one true thing you've been avoiding saying to someone, a worry about a friend, that you were hurt, that you were wrong, and just find the sentence, without saying it yet. Turn it over slowly, the way you'd want to hear it if you were them, taking out the sharp edge and keeping the truth; if you pray, ask for courage and gentleness together, and if not, sit with the sentence until it feels both honest and kind.
Veritas. Latin for truth, and the Dominican motto: truth that is someone to follow, and truth told in charity. Today's word.
Your line: veritas. Pilate walked out on the question; this order stayed to answer it. Go gently.

1234.title: Contemplate and share
1234.hook: the friars' life: prayer and study fill the basin, and preaching is what spills over
1234.howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters pray the Liturgy of the Hours together and set time aside for study, and their preaching and teaching are meant to flow from that prayer; contemplata aliis tradere is quoted as a Dominican motto.

segments.voice: Yesterday, veritas: truth as someone to follow, and truth told in charity. Your line was veritas.

Two ways to move water. A channel takes water in at one end and lets it out the other at the same moment: always flowing, never full. A basin fills first. It holds the water, and only when it's full to the brim does it spill over the edge, and it stays full while it spills. Bernard of Clairvaux, a Cistercian monk, used this picture in a sermon. Too many people, he said, are channels; he wished they were basins. Later a Dominican friar put the same idea into a short Latin phrase, and his order took it up as a motto. Today: fill first, then spill.
screen: `A CHANNEL: ALWAYS FLOWING, NEVER FULL.` → `A BASIN: FILLS FIRST, THEN SPILLS.` → `BERNARD WISHED FOR BASINS.`

segments.voice: The friar was Thomas Aquinas. In his Summa he asks a practical question: what kind of religious life is best? Pure prayer, hidden away? Pure action, out in the streets? Neither by itself, he says. Best is to contemplate, and to hand on to others what you have contemplated. In Latin, contemplari et contemplata aliis tradere. His reason is a lovely image: it is a greater thing to give light than only to shine. A lamp glowing in a closed room is good. A lamp carried into a dark street is better. That's the Dominican shape of life. The friars pray the hours together in choir. They study. Then they go out and preach. The preaching isn't meant to be a performance or a sales pitch. It's overflow, the basin spilling over. Jesus says something close in Matthew, in the Douay-Rheims: "out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh." Whatever fills you is what comes out. But notice the order of the words: contemplate first, then share. A friar who only talks runs dry; a friar who only prays keeps the light in the closet. The phrase also works as a small test. Before you give advice, have you looked long at the thing? And after you've looked long, did anyone else get to see it?
screen: `AQUINAS: WHICH LIFE IS BEST?` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN HAND IT ON.` · `BETTER TO GIVE LIGHT THAN ONLY SHINE.` · `PRAY, STUDY, THEN PREACH.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE ABUNDANCE OF THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Look back over this week's quiet moments, a line from a psalm, a thought on a walk, something from one of these sits, and let one come forward: not the most impressive, the one that still feels warm. Hold it for a few breaths, then bring to mind one person who might need exactly that; if you pray, give thanks for what you received and ask for the right moment to pass it on, and if not, hold the thought and the person side by side.
Contemplate and share. Look long at God, then hand on what you've seen: a Dominican motto, from Thomas Aquinas. Today's word.
Your line: overflow. A basin gives from what it holds, and stays full while it gives. See you tomorrow.

1235.title: The nine ways of prayer
1235.hook: an early book shows Dominic praying with his whole body: bowing, lying prostrate, standing, reading
1235.howItsDone: Catholics pray with posture at Mass, standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration and bowing in the Creed; Dominicans still read and teach the early book on the ways Saint Dominic prayed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, contemplate and share: the basin fills first, then spills over. Your line was overflow.

Dominic left no handbook on how he prayed. What survives is better, in a way: a record of what people saw. Late at night in a church, a man bows low before the altar. Later he's flat on the stone floor, face down. Later still he's on his feet, arms stretched wide, then reaching straight up, as if for something just out of reach. Then he sits with a book open on his knees and talks to it, nodding, sometimes smiling. The brothers noticed. An early little book gathered it all and named it: the nine ways of prayer of Saint Dominic. Today, prayer that doesn't stay in the head.
screen: `NO HANDBOOK, ONLY WITNESSES.` → `BOWING, LYING FLAT, ARMS WIDE.` → `A BOOK OPEN ON HIS KNEES.`

segments.voice: Walk through the ways the little book describes. He bows deeply, as you'd bow to someone you honor. He lies face down, the posture of someone with nothing left to offer but himself. He kneels and stands and kneels again, like a person knocking at a door. He stands with his hands open before him, as if reading from a book. He stretches his arms out like a cross. He reaches up high. He sits and reads quietly, as if in conversation. And walking from town to town, he prays as he goes. The book ties these postures to scripture, and the Psalms are full of them. In the Douay-Rheims: "Let my prayer be directed as incense in thy sight; the lifting up of my hands, as evening sacrifice." Lifted hands, noticed by God. Why would a preacher, a man of words, pray so much with his body? The idea under the little book, in substance, runs both ways: the soul moves the body, and the body in turn stirs the soul. Kneel and you remember you're small. Open your hands and you remember you're receiving. Catholics still do something like this at Mass: standing for the Gospel, kneeling at the consecration, bowing during the Creed. Dominic just did it alone, at night, with no one watching. Except someone was.

segments.voice: Pick a posture you don't usually use: stand with your hands open in front of you, palms up, like an open book, or kneel, or if you're sitting, lift your hands a little from your lap. Stay with it and notice what it does, how open hands feel different from folded ones; if you pray, let the posture be the prayer, perhaps with the psalm's line about lifted hands, and if not, just breathe and notice how your body holds the moment.

1236.title: Study as prayer
1236.hook: the student who sold his books for the hungry built an order where study is a spiritual discipline
1236.howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters set aside regular hours for study as part of their religious life, and the order runs schools and houses of study, where study is treated as preparation for preaching and a form of devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nine ways of prayer: Dominic bowing, lying flat, reaching up, reading. Your line was the body prays.

A young student in Spain owns a stack of books, precious, copied by hand, his margins full of notes. Then famine hits the town, and people are starving in the streets. The early accounts say he sells the books, notes and all, and gives the money to the hungry. Tradition puts a line in his mouth, in substance: how could he study on dead skins while living people died of hunger? The student was Dominic. And here's the twist: the same man went on to found an order with study at the very center of its life. Today, how both can be true.
screen: `A STUDENT, A STACK OF PRECIOUS BOOKS.` → `FAMINE: HE SELLS THEM ALL.` → `THEN BUILDS AN ORDER OF STUDY.`

segments.voice: Start with the Latin word the friars used: studium. It means study, yes, but Latin dictionaries also give zeal, eagerness, devoted attention. Study, in the old sense, is a kind of love: close attention to what you care about. Early Dominican rules took it so seriously that a superior could excuse a brother from other duties so his study wouldn't be broken. Why would a man who sold his books for the hungry protect study like that? Because the books were never the point. People were. A preacher who hasn't studied gives the hungry stones instead of bread. So for Dominicans, study isn't a break from prayer or a hobby. It's a discipline, like fasting. You sit still. You let a hard text be hard. You stay humble before what's true, even when it isn't what you hoped. And you do it so that later, on a street corner or beside a hospital bed, you have something real to give. The Psalms put it in one line. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." A lamp you carry somewhere. That's study as prayer: attention offered to God, for the sake of people. It doesn't need a library. A nurse learning a new procedure, a parent reading up on a child's diagnosis, a teenager wrestling with algebra: done with love and for others, a Dominican might call that studium too.

segments.voice: Choose something small to read right now, the psalm's line about the lamp, a paragraph from the book by your bed, even a page of notes for work, and read it slowly, then again slower, noticing one word you skipped the first time. Ask what it actually says, not what you expected; if you pray, offer this small attention to God and give thanks at the end, and if not, just give the page your full, patient attention.
Study as prayer. In the Dominican tradition, study is zeal and devoted attention, offered to God for the sake of people. Today's word.

1237.title: The rosary story
1237.hook: tradition says Dominic received the rosary; historians say it grew over a long time, much loved by Dominicans
1237.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or together, often on beads, saying an Our Father, a decade of Hail Marys and a Glory Be while meditating on a mystery; Dominican friars and parishes lead it and preach about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, study as prayer: studium, zeal and devoted attention, offered for people. Your line was study is prayer.

It's in paintings, in stained glass, above side altars. A woman in blue, crowned, sits with a child on her lap. Kneeling below her is a friar in a white habit and a black cape. She leans down and hands him a string of beads. The friar is Dominic, the woman is Mary, and the beads are a rosary. It's a beautiful scene, and Dominicans have painted it lovingly. It also raises a question a curious person will eventually ask: did it happen like that? Today, the rosary story, and why the answer comes in two parts.
screen: `A WOMAN IN BLUE, A KNEELING FRIAR.` → `SHE HANDS HIM A STRING OF BEADS.` → `DID IT HAPPEN LIKE THAT?`

segments.voice: Back on day four, you met what the rosary's string is for; today, its story. Part one is the tradition. Tradition says Mary gave the rosary to Dominic, as a help for his preaching in the south of France. Popes and preachers have retold it, and the picture hangs in Dominican churches. Part two is what historians see: a prayer that grew slowly, from many hands. Monks prayed the Psalms. People who couldn't read them prayed Our Fathers instead, counted on strings of beads or knots. Then came the Hail Mary, whose first lines are two greetings from Luke's Gospel stitched together. Gabriel's, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." And Elizabeth's, when Mary visits her: "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Over time people attached scenes to the beads, moments in the lives of Jesus and Mary to think about while the words went by: the mysteries. And the Dominicans? Historians credit them with loving and spreading the rosary widely, preaching it and gathering people to pray it together; a later Dominican preacher also spread the story of Dominic receiving it. So Catholics hold this in different ways. Some take the story as history. Others read it as a picture of something true: the rosary found its home among Dominicans. Either way, the prayer grew like a family recipe, a pinch added by each generation, until nobody can say whose it was. It belongs to all of them.

1238.title: Catherine the Dominican
1238.hook: Catherine of Siena lived as a Dominican laywoman, at home, in a black cloak
1238.howItsDone: Lay Dominicans belong to fraternities attached to the Order of Preachers, making a promise, meeting to pray and study, and serving in ordinary life; Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a Doctor of the Church and read her Dialogue and letters.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rosary story, a prayer that grew from many hands. Your line was a story that grew.

Siena, in Italy. A dyer's house, loud with family, the smell of the vats drifting in from the work yard. One of the daughters won't marry. Her family pushes; she refuses. She doesn't run off to a convent, either. She asks to join a group of local women who wear a white dress and a black cloak, and live in their own homes. For a while she barely leaves a small room in her parents' house. Then she walks out of it, and doesn't stop: sickrooms, prisons, city councils, and eventually the pope's court. Her name was Catherine. Today, the woman in the black cloak.
screen: `SIENA, A DYER'S HOUSE.` → `SHE WON'T MARRY. NO CONVENT, EITHER.` → `A WHITE DRESS, A BLACK CLOAK.`

segments.voice: You met Catherine of Siena back on day eighty-nine; today, the cloak she wore. The women were called the mantellate, from the Italian for a mantle, a cloak. They belonged to the Dominican family as laywomen, doing penance and works of mercy, not as cloistered nuns. Catherine became a mantellata. She lived at home and went out into the city. Her confessor, the Dominican Raymond of Capua, wrote her life, and tells of her nursing the sick and visiting prisoners. In one of her own letters she describes sitting with a young man condemned to death, staying with him to the end. Matthew's Gospel names that kind of love. In the Douay-Rheims: "I was sick, and you visited me: I was in prison, and you came to me." Then came the letters. Catherine dictated letters to kings, city leaders, cardinals, and the pope himself, who was living in Avignon, in France, far from Rome. She wrote to him plainly, with respect and with fire, urging him to come back to Rome and make peace. Her thinking about God and the soul, gathered in a book called the Dialogue, is still read, and the Church calls her a Doctor of the Church, a teacher for everyone. All from a laywoman in a cloak. Being a Dominican, she showed, isn't only for friars and nuns. It's a family with room at the kitchen table.

1239.title: Are these not men? (1511)
1239.hook: Antonio de Montesinos preaches on Hispaniola against the colonists' cruelty to Indigenous people
1239.howItsDone: Dominicans remember Antonio de Montesinos's Advent sermon as part of their tradition of preaching for human dignity, and Catholic teaching on the dignity of every person is often taught alongside the story of Montesinos and Bartolomé de las Casas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, a Dominican laywoman in a black cloak. Your line was the mantellata.

Advent, on the island of Hispaniola, in the Caribbean. A rough church, and in it the leading men of the Spanish colony, who hold Indigenous people as forced laborers in the mines and fields. A Dominican friar named Antonio de Montesinos climbs up to preach. His text is from John's Gospel, John the Baptist describing himself. In the Douay-Rheims: "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness." Then he tells them who the wilderness is. It's them. Today, the sermon, and the question at the heart of it.
screen: `ADVENT, ON HISPANIOLA.` → `THE COLONY'S LEADING MEN IN THE PEWS.` → `A VOICE CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: You met this sermon briefly on day eight hundred thirty-nine; today, its words. It survives because Bartolomé de las Casas wrote it down in his history of the Indies. As he tells it, Montesinos said everyone listening was living in mortal sin because of the cruelty and tyranny they used against these innocent people. Then came the questions, which Las Casas records in substance. By what right do you hold these people in such cruel servitude? Why do you work them until they fall sick and die? Then today's line: are these not men? Do they not have rational souls? Are you not bound to love them as you love yourselves? That last question is Jesus's own command, in the Douay-Rheims: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Montesinos didn't speak alone. Las Casas says the friars of his house agreed on the sermon together and put their names to it. The furious colonists went to the friars' house and demanded he take it back the next Sunday. He came back, climbed up again, and preached the same truth, harder. It didn't end the cruelty. The sermon set off arguments that reached the Spanish court. And one man in that colony, Las Casas himself, who held laborers too, later gave them up, became a Dominican, and spent his life defending Indigenous people. Friars of the Church named the sin of the Church's own people, out loud, to their faces. Veritas, told when it cost something.
screen: `LAS CASAS WROTE IT DOWN.` · `ARE THESE NOT MEN?` · `TAKE IT BACK. HE PREACHED IT AGAIN.` · `LAS CASAS CHANGED HIS LIFE.` · then, large: `LOVE THEM AS YOU LOVE YOURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone in your world who is easy to look past, the person who cleans the office at night, someone talked about as a problem and never as a person, and hold their face, or picture one. Let Montesinos's question sit beside it, are these not people, with a soul and a story; if you pray, pray for them by name if you know it, and if not, simply keep their face in mind.
Are these not men? A Dominican's question to colonists who were working Indigenous people to death. This week ran from veritas to the truth told when it cost something. Today's word.
Your line: are these not men. Asked to the powerful, and asked again the next Sunday. See you tomorrow.
